Treat the declaration as four independent universal facts. After naming them \(P,Q,R,S\), the goal is \((P\leftrightarrow Q)\land(R\leftrightarrow S)\); prove each of \(P,Q,R,S\) once, then assemble both biconditionals without deriving one characterization from the other.

The useful intermediate goals are:

- Connectedness characterization: a space is connected exactly when some connected component is the whole space.
- Total disconnectedness characterization: a space is totally disconnected exactly when every connected component is subsingleton.
- Closed-injective pullback: an injective closed map has a continuous inverse on its range. Since \(s\subseteq\operatorname{range} f\), the preimage \(f^{-1}(s)\) is the continuous image of the preconnected set \(s\) under this inverse, hence is preconnected. The range assumption is essential here.
- Component monotonicity: use the description of `connectedComponentIn F x` as the union/maximal preconnected subset of \(F\) containing \(x\). Any such subset remains admissible after \(F\subseteq G\), yielding
  \[
  \operatorname{connectedComponentIn}(F,x)\subseteq
  \operatorname{connectedComponentIn}(G,x).
  \]

These are standard topology lemmas likely already available under the connected-component and preconnectedness APIs; the explicit `@` syntax should first be mentally reduced to their ordinary formulations.
